context:
This item asks which way to settle a known gap. It does not block the PR.
Goal: a cloud session that cannot reinstall does not waste work on every prompt, and a failed first install does not stay silent.
Problem (rule): debt reinstall-no-backoff. After a failed landing the old install record stays, so the hook retries on every prompt: one `git ls-remote` plus one installer run, with no backoff. A failed first install of a session leaves no record, so no retry runs and the hook prints "install freshness unknown". Whether to leave this as a debt or build a backoff is your call, since a backoff changes what the hook does.
Based on (read): PR 3487 body, "Retry cost for debt reinstall-no-backoff", read by triage at 03:15 CST Nov 15; the coordinator relayed the lane's wording at 03:12 CST. Triage read no code.
Based on (unmeasured): how often a landing fails in a cloud session, and what one installer run costs.
Departs from: main — adds a retry on every prompt after a failed landing, with no limit; a backoff would change that.
Who recommends what: nobody has recommended an option; no star.
Meanwhile: PR 3487 is not held on this answer. The debt stays filed as reinstall-no-backoff.

options.label: Keep it as a debt; build a backoff only after a real incident
options.lose: A cloud session whose install keeps failing runs one ls-remote plus one installer run on every prompt.

options.gain: A failing install stops costing work on every prompt.
options.how: A follow-up lane adds a backoff: after a failed landing the hook waits a set time before the next try, and prints that it is waiting.
options.label: Build a backoff in a follow-up lane now
options.lose: More hook logic to build and test before any failure is seen, and a stale install stays stale for the wait.

title: PR 3487: after a failed reinstall, may the hook keep retrying on every prompt, or should it back off?
why: The hook retries each prompt after a failed landing (one ls-remote plus one installer run). A failed first install leaves no record and no retry. Nothing measures how often this happens.
